A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attention-trajectory study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent-training results, attention measurements, behavioral interventions, and saliency-method comparisons across Atari, Custom Pong, and biomechanical simulations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds replay-buffer, annotation-granularity/noise, and object-size/speed experiments in Appendices I.3 and M.

M1.justification: The h-profile computation, neuron-selection threshold, LRP propagation rules, alternative saliency adaptations, and agent architectures remain unchanged. The five-component framework in v3 Section 3.1 organizes practices already implemented in v1; the new experiments vary evaluation conditions.

E1.justification: Appendix M.2 adds Custom Pong training scenarios with altered ball/paddle sizes and velocities, changing visual and interaction conditions. The four Atari games, original Pong reward variants, and two biomechanical tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain A2C, PPO, DQN, and QR-DQN, together with LRP, Grad, SmoothGrad, and perturbation-based saliency. Replay-buffer configurations are additional ablation conditions, not newly introduced comparison methods.

E3.justification: Substantial new evaluation designs include replay-buffer sizes of 100, 1,000, 100,000, and 1,000,000; four annotation granularities and three corruption types evaluated on 100 observations using Jensen–Shannon distance; and size/speed variants using 50 observations per condition and seed. These extend the protocol rather than replace the original experiments' settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds a replay-buffer ablation linking brick attention to perturbation robustness, tests sensitivity to segmentation granularity and labeling errors, and examines object-size and velocity effects. These address previously untested mechanisms and measurement sensitivities while retaining v1's existing robustness analyses.

E5.justification: The moving-button comparison changes from a two-sample to a paired t-test in the stated methods and results, retaining p = 0.009 and Cohen's d = -1.31 without explaining the pairing. The new annotation study reports three noise repetitions with standard deviations. Existing run counts and ANOSIM permutation settings remain unchanged.

E6.justification: The principal results in Figures 2–4 are retained, but Figures 15 and 25–28 add substantial findings: smaller replay buffers reduce brick attention and improve DQN perturbation robustness; annotation sensitivity depends on granularity; larger balls increase ball attention; and faster balls increase attention to the agent's paddle. These are newly reported results under additional conditions.

T1.justification: The h-profile definitions and saliency derivations, including Equations 1–11 and Appendices A–B, retain their mathematical content. No new theorem or proof is introduced; Jensen–Shannon distance is used as an evaluation metric.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that attention trajectories diagnose algorithmic biases, reward-induced strategies, and reliance on redundant sensory cues beyond performance scores. The later abstract and contribution list foreground a five-component framework, but its functions and central diagnostic claims were already present in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds replay-buffer explanations and explicitly attributes attention differences to both algorithm design and hyperparameters. It also explains granularity-dependent annotation sensitivity and qualifies interpretation through saliency-resolution limits, low-level visual biases, and confounding between perception and task dynamics. Section 3.1 explicitly states that attention profiles alone cannot establish functional feature use.

D1.justification: v3 reports a concrete code repository instead of promising release upon publication. It clarifies the shared actor–critic Fc representation and documents annotation perturbations and environmental scaling factors for the added experiments. Existing architecture, training-hyperparameter, and hardware disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Selder et al. (2026) on visual bias in simulated users and more explicitly relates its aggregation principle to Lapuschkin et al. (2019). Most other citation changes update bibliographic information for existing works, including the observational-overfitting reference.

P1.justification: v3 adds a five-part framework exposition, rewrites the abstract and selected introductory passages, expands explanations and limitations, and edits terminology and citations. Most existing prose and the overall three-case-study narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned around the five-component framework, and five experimental figures are added: Figure 15 and Figures 25–28. Existing appendix illustrations are redistributed, including the Atari object illustration moving from Figure 7 to Figure 13. The principal result plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 already provides behavioral and cross-saliency validation. v3 strengthens it with targeted replay-buffer and measurement-sensitivity experiments, clearer methodological explanations, explicit limitations, and reported code access. The overall gain is limited by the single-agent annotation study, unresolved perception-versus-dynamics confounding, and the unexplained switch to paired testing.
